title: TrailGuard AI cameras in the Kanha-Pench corridor transmit tiger alerts to researchers and forest officials 30 to 42 seconds after detection in a 2022 pilot
summary: BioScience 2023: 12 TrailGuard AI cameras ran in the Kanha-Pench corridor, Madhya Pradesh, mid-May to mid-July 2022 (591 trap nights); tiger notifications arrived 30 to 42 seconds after detection.
account: Dertien et al. reported in BioScience (published 14 September 2023) that 12 TrailGuard AI camera-alert systems ran in the Kanha-Pench corridor, Madhya Pradesh, from mid-May to mid-July 2022 (591 trap nights). The cameras run embedded AI on an Intel Myriad chip to detect tigers and humans and transmit only images of interest; researchers and forest department officials received tiger notifications 30 to 42 seconds after detection. AFP (Taipei Times, 6 October 2023) reported the study's claim that the cameras were 'immediately effective, picking up a tiger just 300 meters from a village'. The Hindu (16 September 2023) reported the Madhya Pradesh deployment and quoted H.S. Negi of the Global Tiger Forum on plans to incorporate the system in other tiger reserves. The paper's second site, Dudhwa Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh, where a unit captured armed poachers, is recorded separately as AIBD-0318. No forest department document on the pilot was fetched. The date used is the BioScience publication date.
purpose: Real-time detection of tigers and humans for human-wildlife conflict early warning and anti-poaching; the reported detections and follow-up were the intended use.
system: TrailGuard AI camera-alert system with embedded AI (Intel Myriad processor; detectors trained with CVEDIA synthetic renderings)
developer: RESOLVE (design) with CVEDIA Ltd (AI training); units manufactured by Nightjar
deployer: Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh forest departments with Clemson University, Wildlife Institute of India and Global Tiger Forum
segment: State forest departments and conservation research partners
taxonomy_note: Tiger protection and anti-poaching fit environmental sustainability. The peer-reviewed paper is co-authored by RESOLVE and CVEDIA staff (vendor-affiliated); the arrests and conviction are reported only through the manufacturer's representative and an unnamed participant in a single news report, not by a forest department or court. Distinct from the Similipal record (AIBD-0102).

ratings.reason: No identified individual beneficiary; villagers near three units are mentioned only as sources of daily notifications.
Researchers and forest department officials received tiger alerts 30 to 42 seconds after detection during the two-month pilot; no action taken on an alert is documented.
No measured effect on human-wildlife conflict in the two-month pilot of 12 cameras.

ai_role.statement: Embedded AI on the camera selected and transmitted images of tigers and humans within 30 to 42 seconds, the mechanism documented in the developer-affiliated BioScience paper; whether any alert changed what villagers or officials did is not documented.

evidence.quote: We successfully captured and transmitted the first images of tigers using cameras with embedded AI and detected poachers.

evidence.title: AI of the tiger: Tiny camera 'protects' predator - and people

produced_by: Camera units with on-device detectors for tigers and humans placed on trails
Cellular or satellite transmission to officials' phones and email
Forest department staff willing to act on transmitted images
Research consortium funding (Tigers United, Clemson, Khosla grant)
must_hold: Transmission path within cell range or via the slower protocol
Detector accuracy high enough to avoid alert fatigue
Investigative follow-up by forest and police authorities
Battery life and concealment of units
